{{Short description|Stream cipher}}
{{Distinguish|ATSC A/52}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=October 2012}}
'''A5/2''' is a [[stream cipher]] used to provide voice privacy in the [[GSM]] [[Cell phone|cellular telephone]] protocol. It was designed in 1992-1993 (finished March 1993) as a replacement for the relatively stronger (but still weak) [[A5/1]], to allow the GSM standard to be exported to countries "with restrictions on the import of products with cryptographic security features".<ref>{{Cite web|last=Security Algorithms Group of Experts (SAGE)|date=March 1996|title=ETR 278 - Report on the specification and evaluation of the GSM cipher algorithm A5/2|url=https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_etr/200_299/278/01_60/etr_278e01p.pdf|url-status=live|website=European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI)|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131204061251/http://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_etr/200_299/278/01_60/etr_278e01p.pdf |archive-date=December 4, 2013 }}</ref>

The cipher is based on a combination of four [[linear-feedback shift register]]s with irregular clocking and a [[non-linear]] combiner.

In 1999, [[Ian Goldberg]] and [[David A. Wagner]] [[Cryptanalysis|cryptanalyzed]] A5/2 in the same month it was reverse engineered, and showed that it was extremely weak – so much so that low end equipment can probably break it in real time.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Goldberg|first1=Ian|last2=Wagner|first2=David|last3=Green|first3=Lucky|date=August 26, 1999|title=The (Real-Time) Cryptanalysis of A5/2|url=https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~daw/tmp/a52-slides.ps|url-status=live|website=David Wagner's page at UC Berkeley Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421131010/https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~daw/tmp/a52-slides.ps |archive-date=April 21, 2021 }}</ref>

In 2003, Elad Barkan, [[Eli Biham]] and Nathan Keller presented a ciphertext-only attack based on the [[Error correction code|error correcting codes]] used in GSM communication. They also demonstrated a vulnerability in the GSM protocols that allows a [[man-in-the-middle attack]] to work whenever the mobile phone supports A5/2, regardless of whether it was actually being used.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Barkan|first1=Elad|last2=Biham|first2=Eli|last3=Keller|first3=Nathan |title=Advances in Cryptology - CRYPTO 2003 |chapter=Instant Ciphertext-Only Cryptanalysis of GSM Encrypted Communication |date=2003|editor-last=Boneh|editor-first=Dan |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=2729|language=en|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|publisher=Springer|pages=600–616|doi=10.1007/978-3-540-45146-4_35|isbn=978-3-540-45146-4|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Since July 1, 2006, the [[GSM Association|GSMA]] (GSM Association) mandated that GSM Mobile Phones will not support the A5/2 Cipher any longer, due to its weakness, and the fact that [[A5/1]] is deemed mandatory by the [[3GPP]] association. In July 2007, the [[3GPP]] has approved a change request to prohibit the implementation of A5/2 in any new mobile phones, stating: "It is mandatory for A5/1 and non encrypted mode to be implemented in mobile stations. It is prohibited to implement A5/2 in mobile stations."<ref>{{Cite web|last=3GPP TSG-SA WG3 (Security) Meeting #48|date=18 September 2007|title=SP-070671 - Prohibiting A5/2 in mobile stations and other clarifications regarding A5 algorithm support|url=https://portal.3gpp.org/ngppapp/CreateTdoc.aspx?mode=view&contributionUid=SP-070671|url-status=live|website=3GPP Change Requests Portal|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421125343/https://portal.3gpp.org/ngppapp/CreateTdoc.aspx?mode=view&contributionUid=SP-070671 |archive-date=April 21, 2021 }}</ref> If the network does not support A5/1 then an unencrypted connection can be used.
